# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has created a pressing need for large-bore vascular access in patients who lack suitable transfemoral arterial corridors. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), in particular, has driven innovation in alternative access, as a substantial minority of patients present with small, calcified, or tortuous iliofemoral arteries [1,2]. Transcaval access—the percutaneous creation of a controlled communication between the inferior vena cava (IVC) and the abdominal aorta—emerged as an ingenious solution that exploits the venous system to deliver devices into the aorta [3,4]. This review summarizes the rationale, technique, evidence base, and future directions of transcaval access.

## Rationale and Anatomical Basis

Traditional alternative access routes for TAVR, including transapical, transaortic, subclavian, and transcarotid approaches, each carry distinct procedural and morbidity profiles [5,6]. Transapical access has been associated with greater myocardial injury and worse outcomes compared with transfemoral approaches [7]. Transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous, non-surgical alternative that avoids thoracotomy and general anesthesia in many cases [8]. The anatomical premise is that the infrarenal abdominal aorta lies in close apposition to the IVC, and that retroperitoneal bleeding into a relatively low-pressure space is often self-limiting because of tamponade and the pressure gradient favoring aorto-caval flow [9,10]. Preprocedural computed tomography is essential to identify a calcium-free aortic target and an adequate apposition zone [11].

## Technique

The technique was pioneered and systematically described by Lederman and colleagues at the National Institutes of Health [3,12]. An electrified guidewire—typically a stiff 0.014-inch coronary wire energized with electrosurgical current—is advanced from the IVC across into a snare positioned in the aorta, creating the crossing [12,13]. The wire is then exchanged for a stiff support wire, and the large-bore sheath is advanced across the aortocaval tract to deliver the valve [14]. At the conclusion of the procedure, the tract is closed using a nitinol occluder device, most commonly an Amplatzer duct occluder or muscular ventricular septal defect occluder [15,16]. Residual aortocaval flow is common immediately but typically resolves or remains clinically inconsequential [17].

## Clinical Evidence

The prospective multicenter Transcaval Access for TAVR study enrolled 100 patients with prohibitive transfemoral access and demonstrated high procedural success (99%) with acceptable safety, establishing transcaval access as feasible across institutions [18]. Registry data and single-center series have corroborated these findings, reporting successful valve delivery and tract closure in the large majority of patients [19,20]. Comparative analyses suggest that transcaval access yields outcomes at least comparable to other alternative access routes, with shorter recovery and the advantage of conscious sedation [21,22]. Mortality and stroke rates in contemporary series are consistent with high-risk TAVR populations undergoing alternative access [23].

The principal complication is bleeding, including retroperitoneal hematoma and the need for transfusion or, less commonly, endovascular or surgical intervention [24]. Most bleeding events are manageable, and the predicted catastrophic exsanguination has been rare in practice [25]. Failure of tract closure and persistent aortocaval fistula are uncommon but require monitoring, as high-output fistulae can lead to heart failure [26].

## Applications Beyond TAVR

Although developed primarily for TAVR, transcaval access has been applied to other large-bore needs, including endovascular aneurysm repair, mechanical circulatory support cannulation, and transcatheter mitral interventions [27,28]. The principle of crossing between adjacent vascular structures has also informed broader interventional techniques and device development for tract closure [29].

## Future Directions

Refinements in dedicated crossing and closure devices, improved imaging-based patient selection, and growing operator experience are likely to enhance safety [30]. As transfemoral access becomes feasible in more patients with smaller-profile delivery systems, transcaval access will remain a valuable option for the subset with prohibitive anatomy. Continued registry data collection and comparative effectiveness studies are needed to define its precise role within the alternative access armamentarium.

## Conclusion

Transcaval access is a creative, fully percutaneous solution to the challenge of large-bore aortic access in patients without suitable transfemoral arterial routes. Supported by a growing evidence base, it offers favorable outcomes with manageable bleeding risk when guided by careful imaging and meticulous technique. It represents an important addition to the structural heart interventionalist's toolkit.
